stages.title: Advanced grammar
stages.hook: From one root ʿ-l-m we get "knew", "taught", "learned" and "informed". What do you think changes the meaning?
explain: Arabic verbs come in forms (awzān), each a pattern on the root. Form I is the base: ʿalima (he knew). Form II doubles the middle letter: ʿallama (he taught, "made know"). Form IV adds a- : aʿlama (he informed). Form V adds ta- and doubling: taʿallama (he learned). Form X adds ista-: istaʿlama (he inquired, "sought to know").

Each form adds a typical meaning: II often intensifies or makes causative, III is "do with someone" (kātaba, correspond), V is reflexive of II, VI is reciprocal (tabādala, exchange), VII is passive or reflexive, X means "seek or consider".

Nouns follow patterns as well: ʿālim (scholar, doer), maʿlūm (known, thing done), ʿilm (knowledge), muʿallim (teacher), mutaʿallim (learner). In formal Arabic the noun endings show case: -u nominative, -a accusative, -i genitive.
stages.mnemonic: Same three consonants, new costume: each form wears a different pattern.
sentences: The teacher taught the students the lesson.
I learned Arabic at the university.
The scholar wrote a long book.

gq.q: Which form of ʿ-l-m means "to teach" (make someone know)?
gq.why: Doubling the middle letter in Form II often adds a causative meaning.

gq.q: What do the endings -u, -a, -i on nouns mark in formal Arabic?
gq.why: These short vowels show the noun's function in the sentence.

panel.q: A learner sees kātaba (Form III) and guesses "he wrote with someone". Why is this reasonable?
o: Form III often means doing the action with or to another person
panel.why: Form III (fāʿala) often involves another person, as in correspondence.

panel.q: Why is "al-muʿallimu" (nominative) in ʿallama al-muʿallimu aṭ-ṭullāba but "aṭ-ṭullāba" (accusative)?
o: The teacher is the subject; the students are the object
panel.why: Case marks the role: subject takes -u, direct object takes -a.

panel.q: Describe how roots and forms help a learner build vocabulary.
panel.model: A root gives the core idea and each pattern or form adds a typical meaning, so knowing a few patterns lets you work out many new words from known roots.
panel.why: Root and pattern make Arabic morphology predictable.

teach.model: Arabic verbs are built on a root with patterns called forms. Form II doubles the middle letter and often means to cause. Nouns in formal Arabic have case endings.

points.ask: How is a new verb formed?

stages.title: Complex sentence patterns
stages.hook: "Indeed knowledge is light." In Arabic, one small word at the start changes the case of the next noun. Which one?
explain: Two groups of particles change the grammar of a nominal sentence. Kāna and its sisters (kāna, aṣbaḥa, laysa, mā zāla) keep the subject nominative and put the predicate in the accusative: kāna al-jawwu bāridan, "the weather was cold". Inna and its sisters (inna, anna, lākinna, layta, laʿalla) put the subject in the accusative and keep the predicate nominative: inna al-ʿilma nūrun, "indeed knowledge is light".
Conditionals use idhā (real, likely), in (possible) and law (unreal): law darasta lanajaḥta, "if you had studied, you would have succeeded". The answer clause after law often has la-.
The verbal noun (maṣdar) turns an action into a noun: kitāba (writing), dirāsa (study). This is widely used in formal texts to compress ideas.
stages.mnemonic: Kāna keeps the subject, changes the predicate; inna changes the subject, keeps the predicate.
items: if you had studied, you would have succeeded
sentences: If I had known of the matter, I would have come.
The weather became cold in winter.

gq.q: After inna, what case does the subject take?
gq.why: Inna and its sisters put the subject in the accusative.

gq.q: Which particle expresses an unreal condition such as "if you had studied"?
gq.why: Law introduces unreal or contrary-to-fact conditions.

panel.q: In kāna al-jawwu bāridan, why does bāridan end in -an?
o: Kāna puts the predicate in the accusative
panel.why: After kāna the predicate is accusative.

panel.q: What is the difference between idhā darasta najaḥta and law darasta lanajaḥta?
o: The first is a real or likely condition; the second is unreal or past and contrary to fact
panel.why: Idhā for real conditions; law for hypothetical or unreal ones.

panel.q: Why is inna al-ʿilma nūrun different in case from al-ʿilmu nūrun?
panel.model: After inna the subject al-ʿilm becomes accusative (al-ʿilma). Without inna, in a simple nominal sentence, the subject is nominative (al-ʿilmu).
panel.why: Inna changes the case of its subject.

teach.model: Kāna and its sisters change the predicate to accusative. Inna and its sisters change the subject to accusative. Law is used for unreal conditions.

stages.title: Extended conversations
stages.hook: A guest arrives at an Arab home. The host says "the house is your house". What do they mean?
explain: Hospitality is central in Arab cultures. A host says tafaḍḍal (please, go ahead) and al-baytu baytuka (the house is your house). The guest thanks the host with shukran ʿalā ḥusn ḍiyāfatikum, "thanks for your good hospitality".

For an invitation: awaddu an adʿuwaka ilā l-ʿashāʾ, "I would like to invite you to dinner". Verbs like awaddu (I would like) and an are followed by a short present verb ending in -a: an adʿuwaka. To apologise: aʿtadhiru ʿani t-taʾakhkhur, "I apologise for being late".

Extended talk also needs question forms for work and help: mādhā taʿmalu? (what do you do?), hal yumkinuka musāʿadatī? (could you help me?). Keep switching between formal phrases and warmer dialect when your hosts do.
stages.mnemonic: Tafaḍḍal: "after you": the host's gift of a first move.
items: I would like to invite you to dinner
sentences: I would like to invite you to dinner on Friday.
Please come in, the house is your house.

o: Warm welcome: make yourself at home
It is my house, not yours
gq.why: It is a traditional phrase of hospitality.

gq.q: After "awaddu an", which verb form follows?
gq.why: An is followed by a present verb in the subjunctive.

panel.q: Why does a guest often refuse the first offer of food in some Arab contexts and then accept?
o: Politeness conventions: a host repeats the offer and the guest then accepts
Because they cannot read the menu
panel.why: Customs of modesty and generosity differ by place, but repeated offers are common.

panel.q: Which phrase best thanks a host after dinner?
panel.why: This directly thanks them for their hospitality.

panel.q: Why might you switch between MSA and a dialect when talking with a host?
panel.model: MSA is polite and widely understood; the local dialect is warmer and what the host uses at home, so using some of it shows friendliness.
panel.why: Register shifts signal respect and warmth.

teach.model: Hosts say tafaḍḍal and al-baytu baytuka. Guests thank them with shukran ʿalā ḥusn ḍiyāfatikum. Use awaddu an to invite politely.

points.ask: How do I invite someone politely?

stages.title: Formal and informal registers
stages.hook: You write to a minister and to your best friend. Which Arabic would change most: the words, the grammar or the dialect?
explain: Arabic registers range from formal MSA to local dialects. Letters and official texts open with formulas such as sayyidī al-muḥtaram (Dear Sir) or taḥiyya ṭayyiba wa-baʿdu (greetings, and then) and end with wa-tafaḍḍalū bi-qabūli fāʾiqi l-iḥtirām (please accept my highest respect).

Dialects are used in speech, songs and films. How are you? is izzayyak in Egyptian Arabic, kīfak in Levantine, shlōnak in Gulf and Iraqi Arabic, and lābās in Moroccan Arabic (Darija). Dialect "now" is dilwaʾtī in Egyptian, and "I want" is ʿāyiz (Egyptian m.), biddī (Levantine), abghā (Gulf) and bghīt (Moroccan).

Linguists call this diglossia: two linked varieties used in different situations. Many Arabs also mix them (code-switching) in conversation, for example using MSA formulas inside a dialect conversation.
stages.mnemonic: Formal opens with a ribbon; informal with a wave.
sentences: I hope you will set a time for a meeting.

gq.q: Which phrase is Egyptian Arabic for "how are you?"
gq.why: Izzayyak is Egyptian; kīfak is Levantine; shlōnak Gulf/Iraqi; kayfa ḥāluka MSA.

o: Two related varieties used for different purposes: formal and everyday
gq.why: In Arabic, MSA and the dialects have different roles.

panel.q: Why would "izzayyak" look out of place in a formal letter?
o: It belongs to spoken dialect, not to written formal register
It is incorrect Arabic in every context
panel.why: Formal letters use MSA conventions.

panel.q: A speaker uses mostly dialect but adds an MSA phrase. What is this called?
panel.why: Mixing varieties in one conversation is code-switching.

panel.q: Explain why a Moroccan and an Iraqi can find each other's dialects hard but can both read the same newspaper.
panel.model: Written and news Arabic is MSA, shared by all; the spoken dialects have developed differently by region, so they can be hard to understand across distant regions.
panel.why: MSA unifies writing; dialects diverge in speech.

teach.model: Formal letters use MSA formulas like sayyidī al-muḥtaram and end with respect. Everyday speech uses dialects such as Egyptian izzayyak. Always name the dialect.

points.ask: What do people say in speech?

stages.title: Reading articles and literature
stages.hook: A famous line says "The horses, the night and the desert know me." Who might say this, and why would it sound grand?
explain: Arabic reading ranges from news to poetry. Newspaper headlines often drop the verb ("President to visit Cairo") and use the passive: turjimat ar-riwāya, "the novel was translated". The passive is formed by changing the vowels inside the verb: kataba → kutiba.

Classical poetry is built on the qaṣīda, a long poem with one meter (baḥr) and one rhyme (qāfiya) at the end of every line. Al-Mutanabbi (10th century) is among the most quoted poets: "al-khaylu wa-l-laylu wa-l-baydāʾu taʿrifunī wa-s-sayfu wa-r-rumḥu wa-l-qirṭāsu wa-l-qalamu", where "pen" and "sword" stand together as marks of his life.

Modern Arabic literature includes the novel, introduced in the 20th century. Naguib Mahfouz of Egypt won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. When you read, notice the genre first: news is direct, poetry is dense and figurative.
stages.mnemonic: Qaṣīda: one meter and one rhyme, like a drum beat down the page.
sentences: The horses, the night and the desert know me; the sword, the spear, the paper and the pen.
The newspaper published the article yesterday.
The novel was translated into many languages.

o: A long poem with one meter and rhyme
gq.why: The qaṣīda is the main form of classical Arabic poetry.

gq.q: Which Arab writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988?

panel.q: Why is "turjimat" (it was translated) a passive?
o: The vowels inside the verb change and the doer is not named
panel.why: Arabic passive is formed by internal vowel change.

panel.q: Why does an Arabic poem have a rhyme (qāfiya) at the end of every line?
o: It is a defining feature of the classical form
panel.why: The consistent end-rhyme is typical of the qaṣīda.

panel.q: Name one difference between reading a news article and reading a poem.
panel.model: News is direct and gives facts; a poem is dense and figurative, using images, rhythm and rhyme.
panel.why: Genre changes how we read.

teach.model: Newspapers use short headlines and the passive. Classical poems called qaṣīda have one meter and one rhyme. Naguib Mahfouz was a Nobel Prize winning novelist.

points.ask: What is special about news Arabic?
Who is a famous modern writer?

stages.title: Essay and correspondence writing
stages.hook: You write an email to a university in Arabic. Which opening and closing show respect?
explain: A formal email or letter has a clear shape: salutation, subject (al-mawḍūʿ), purpose, details, request and closing. Useful phrases: akhtubu ilaykum bi-khuṣūṣi ... (I am writing to you regarding ...), murfaqan (attached), fī intiẓāri raddikum (awaiting your reply), maʿa aṭyabi t-taḥiyyāt (with best regards).

An essay (maqāla) has an introduction (muqaddima), a body of paragraphs (fiqra) and a conclusion (khātima). Use connectors from the previous level and be careful with agreement: noun, adjective and verb must match in gender and number.
Prefer clear, complete sentences. Use the Arabic comma (،) and semicolon (؛). Avoid mixing dialect into formal writing unless you are quoting someone.
stages.mnemonic: Letter: Hello, Purpose, Details, Request, Goodbye: HPDRG.
sentences: I am writing to you regarding the course.
I look forward to your kind reply.

gq.q: Which word means "attached" in an email?
Which punctuation mark is the Arabic comma?
gq.why: The comma is ، (written reversed compared to English).

panel.q: Why is the plural "kum" (ilaykum) used to address one official?
o: It means there are many readers
panel.why: Using the plural for a single person shows respect in formal letters.

panel.q: A student's essay has no conclusion. What should be added?
o: A khātima summarising the main ideas
panel.why: An essay needs a summarising conclusion.

panel.q: List the main parts of a formal Arabic letter or email.
panel.model: Salutation, subject and purpose, details, request, and a polite closing.
panel.why: Formal letters follow a conventional order.

teach.model: A formal letter has a greeting, a subject, details, a request and a polite closing. An essay has an introduction, paragraphs and a conclusion. Use bi-khuṣūṣ for regarding.

points.ask: How do I give the purpose?

stages.title: Translation fundamentals
stages.hook: Arabic has no word for "is" and puts the verb first. How could a translator move that into English?
explain: Translating is not swapping words. Arabic often begins with the verb (VSO) and leaves out "is": al-bayt kabīr (the house big). To translate into English, add "is" and put the subject first. In the other direction, an English "I have" becomes ʿindī / ladayya (literally "at me").

Some modern words are borrowed (tilifizyūn) and some are coined from Arabic roots: ḥāsūb (computer, from the root ḥ-s-b, "calculate"), hātif (telephone, literally "caller"), tilfāz (television). Language academies in Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad propose these terms, and speakers often choose between them.

A good translator reads the whole text, finds the meaning, then writes natural English. Literal translation can hide meaning (for example idioms); free translation can lose details. Check key words, tone and register.
stages.mnemonic: Translate meaning, not words: the sentence is a house, not a pile of bricks.
sentences: The translator reads the text carefully.
Translation is more than replacing words.
I use the dictionary every day.

gq.q: How is "I have a car" said in Arabic?
gq.why: Arabic uses ʿinda or ladā + pronoun for possession.

o: A word translated part by part from another language
gq.why: A calque copies the structure of a foreign expression.

panel.q: The Arabic sentence "al-jawwu ḥārr" has no verb. How should you translate it?
panel.why: English requires the verb "is" even though Arabic omits it.

panel.q: Why is a literal translation of "ʿalā ʿaynī wa-raʾsī" a risk?
o: It is an idiom meaning gladly
panel.why: Idioms need meaning-based translation.

panel.q: Why does a translator need to think about register as well as meaning?
panel.model: The same idea can be formal or informal; a good translation keeps the tone and suits the audience and situation.
panel.why: Meaning includes style and tone.

teach.model: Translating means carrying meaning, not words. Arabic omits the word is and often puts the verb first. A translator adds is, reorders and checks tone.

points.ask: What should a translator carry across?
What is different in Arabic grammar?

stages.title: Regional varieties and cultural context
stages.hook: Why can an Egyptian film be enjoyed in Kuwait or Morocco, but a Moroccan street conversation may confuse an Iraqi?
explain: The Arabic dialects form a continuum. Major groups are: Egyptian (widely understood thanks to film and TV), Levantine (Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine), Gulf (Arabian Peninsula) and Maghrebi (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, with many Amazigh and French loanwords). Iraqi and Sudanese Arabic are other major groups.

Differences show up in sounds, words and grammar. "What?" is ēh in Egyptian and shū in Levantine; "I want" is biddī (Levantine), ʿāyiz (Egyptian m.), abghā (Gulf) and bghīt (Moroccan). Over a large distance, speakers may find each other's dialect hard, but MSA gives a shared written base.
Cultural context matters: greetings, humour, hospitality and music differ by region. Name the dialect when you quote it, and avoid saying that one is "better" than another.
stages.mnemonic: One written roof, many spoken rooms.
sentences: Dialects differ, but they share one written language.
Egyptian films are understood in the Arab world.
I want some water, please (Levantine Arabic).

gq.q: Which dialect group is known for many Amazigh (Berber) and French loanwords?
gq.why: The Maghreb has contact with Amazigh languages and French.

gq.q: Why are Egyptian dialect films widely understood?
o: Egypt's film and TV industry has long exported across the Arab world
Egyptian is the only legal dialect
Egyptian is the same as MSA
All Arabs learn it in school
gq.why: Wide circulation made the Egyptian dialect familiar.

panel.q: Why is it risky to say "biddī" in Cairo and expect to be fully understood?
o: It is Levantine; Egyptians say ʿāyiz or ʿāwiz
panel.why: Many people will guess it, but it is a dialect word from another region.

panel.q: What does the dialect continuum mean?
o: Neighbouring dialects are similar, and differences grow with distance
Dialects are languages of different families
panel.why: Gradual change means close dialects are mutually clear.

panel.q: Why does MSA remain useful even though everybody speaks a dialect at home?
panel.model: MSA is the shared written and formal language used in schools, news and books across the Arab world, so people from different dialects can understand each other.
panel.why: MSA is the common standard.

teach.model: Arabic has major dialect groups: Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf and Maghrebi. They differ in words and sounds. MSA is the shared written language.

stages.title: Structured debates and presentations
stages.hook: In a debate you must give an opinion, a reason and an example. Which Arabic words can start each one?
explain: A structured argument uses signposts: fī raʾyī (in my opinion), li-anna (because), ḥujja (argument), dalīl (evidence), min jiha ukhrā (on the other hand), urīdu an uḍīfa (I would like to add), akhluṣu ilā (I conclude that). Rebut respectfully: lā uwāfiqu ʿalā dhālika li-anna ...

A short presentation in Arabic has a greeting (as-salāmu ʿalaykum, ayyuhā l-ḥuḍūru l-karīm, "dear audience"), a topic statement, three points with examples, and a thank-you. The audience expects a calm, clear voice; use MSA for a formal debate.
Practise good delivery: speak clearly with correct long vowels, vary your tone, and use the dual or plural forms of "you" when you address several people.
stages.mnemonic: Opinion, reason, example, answer: ORE-A, four steps up a ladder.
sentences: In my opinion, reading is more useful than television.
On the other hand, technology saves time.
I would like to add one point.

gq.q: Which phrase introduces your own view?
Which phrase signals a contrasting point?

panel.q: A debater says "dalīl" after a claim. What is expected next?
panel.why: Dalīl means proof or evidence.

panel.q: Which is the most respectful way to disagree?
panel.why: Giving a reason keeps disagreement polite.

panel.q: Describe a simple structure for a short debate speech in Arabic.
panel.model: State your opinion, give reasons and evidence with an example, answer the other side with min jiha ukhrā, and finish with a conclusion.
panel.why: Clear structure persuades.

teach.model: State your opinion with fī raʾyī, give a reason with li-anna, add evidence (dalīl) and an example. Use min jihatin ukhrā for the other side and end with a conclusion.

points.ask: How do I give an opinion?
How do I answer and finish?
